## [Quick poll — do nonparametric models have parameters?]{.lang-en}[小テスト — ノンパラメトリックモデルにパラメータはある？]{.lang-ja} {.poll-slide}

::: {.lang-en}
Last week: **Bayesian nonparametric** models (CRP, Dirichlet process, GPs). Do they have parameters?
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
先週：**ベイズ・ノンパラメトリック**モデル（CRP・ディリクレ過程・GP）。パラメータはある？
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.lang-en}
- **A.** Yes — infinitely many
- **B.** Yes — just a few
- **C.** No — it's called *non*parametric for a reason
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
- **A.** ある — 無限個
- **B.** ある — 少数だけ
- **C.** ない — だから*ノン*パラメトリック
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Commit before reveal. Sourced from the SP25 "Intro to Bayes Nonparametrics" quiz (Q1, gf28c347…). The point of opening here: "infinitely many parameters" is exactly the mindset we need today — modern nets are wildly overparameterized, and Week 10 already showed us (via NNGP/NTK) that the infinite-width limit is a GP. Hold the answer to the next slide.
:::

## [Reveal]{.lang-en}[答え]{.lang-ja} {.poll-reveal}

[**A — infinitely many.**]{.lang-en .yellow}[**A — 無限個。**]{.lang-ja .yellow}

::: {.lang-en}
A nonparametric model doesn't *fix* how many parameters it has — it lets the number **grow with the data**. Hold that thought: today's networks are also enormous, and last week we saw the infinite-width limit *is* a Gaussian process.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
ノンパラメトリックモデルはパラメータ数を*固定しない* — データとともに**増やす**。この発想を覚えておいて：今日のネットワークも巨大で、先週見たように無限幅の極限は*まさに*ガウス過程だった。
:::

::: {.notes}
"Nonparametric" = capacity grows with data, not "no parameters." The bridge to today: overparameterization is the norm now, and we already have a Bayesian handle on its limit (GP). One beat, move on.
:::

## [Our standing critic: Lake et al. 2017]{.lang-en}[常設の批評者：Lake et al. 2017]{.lang-ja}

::: {.lang-en}
This week's reading — *Building machines that learn and think like people* — is the **"what's missing from deep learning"** case. We'll keep a running **scorecard**: does each idea today address the critique, or dodge it?

- Their asks: **compositionality**, **causality**, **learning-to-learn**, **intuitive physics/psychology**.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
今週の課題論文 — *人間のように学び考える機械をつくる* — は**「深層学習に何が欠けているか」**の主張。**採点表**を持ち歩く：今日の各アイデアはこの批判に答えるか、かわすか？

- 彼らの要求：**構成性**・**因果性**・**学習の学習**・**直観物理/心理**。
:::

[The charge isn't new: Lake et al. modernize **Fodor & Pylyshyn (1988)**, who argued neural nets lack the **systematicity** of symbolic thought — anyone who can think "John loves Mary" can also think "Mary loves John." A **2025** re-test at the end asks whether today's models close the gap.]{.lang-en .dim}[この批判は新しくない：Lake らは **Fodor & Pylyshyn (1988)** — ニューラルネットは記号的思考の**体系性**を欠くという主張 — を現代化したもの。最後に **2025年**の再検証で、今のモデルがその差を埋めたかを問う。]{.lang-ja .dim}

::: {.notes}
Set up the critical spine. Lake et al. is the required reading and the honest counterweight to hype — we teach the machinery AND ask whether it does what the critique says minds do. Name the lineage (fact-check rule): Lake et al. 2017 is the deep-learning-era restatement of the classic connectionism critique — Fodor & Pylyshyn (1988), "Connectionism and cognitive architecture," on systematicity/compositionality. I revisit this scorecard in the Represent block, the ICL block, and the close — where a 2025 multimodal re-test (Schulze Buschoff et al.) supplies fresh evidence. This is the "teach it critically" stance across a 1988 → 2017 → 2025 arc, not a rubber stamp.
:::

# [Represent I — connectionism]{.lang-en}[表現 I — コネクショニズム]{.lang-ja} {.section-break background-image="../../sds-reveal/sds_frame.png" background-size="cover"}

::: {.notes}
Block 2, REPRESENT. Point at the "features" box of the master map. The idea: cognition (and computation) as the emergent behavior of many simple units — and the payoff is distributed representations, which is what makes learned features special.
:::

## [Emergence: order from simple units]{.lang-en}[創発：単純な要素からの秩序]{.lang-ja}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.lang-en}
- A **termite mound** — meters tall, ventilated, temperature-regulated — is built by thousands of termites with **no architect** and no blueprint.
- Each unit follows tiny local rules; the structure is **emergent**.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
- **シロアリの塚** — 数メートル、換気され、温度調節される — は**設計者なし**で数千匹が作る。
- 各個体は小さな局所ルールに従い、構造は**創発する**。
:::
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.lang-en}
**Connectionism** (Parallel Distributed Processing): model cognition as computation over **many interconnected simple units** — each unit's activity depends only on the units feeding it. Loosely neuron-inspired.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**コネクショニズム**（並列分散処理）：認知を**多数の相互接続された単純な要素**上の計算としてモデル化 — 各要素の活動は入力元の要素だけに依存する。ゆるくニューロンに着想。
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The emergence motivation (SP25's honeycomb/termite framing, kept — it's memorable). Define connectionism / PDP here at first use: computation over many simple interconnected units, neuron-inspired but not a neuroscience claim. McClelland/Rumelhart/Hinton 1986 is the origin. Two-column: emergence example beside the definition.
:::

## [The artificial neuron]{.lang-en}[人工ニューロン]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/sp25/neuron_activation.png){fig-align="center" width="62%"}

::: {.lang-en}
One unit: $a_i = g\!\left(\sum_j w_{ij}\, a_j\right)$ — a **weighted sum** of its inputs, squashed by an **activation function** $g$. The weights $w_{ij}$ are what the network learns.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
一つの要素：$a_i = g\!\left(\sum_j w_{ij}\, a_j\right)$ — 入力の**重み付き和**を**活性化関数** $g$ で押しつぶす。重み $w_{ij}$ こそネットワークが学習するもの。$\sum$ は総和、$w_{ij}$ は結合重み。
:::

::: {.notes}
Define the neuron equation — first use of Σ in a while, so gloss it (weighted sum) in the JA caption and say it aloud. g = activation function; w_ij = the learned weights. This is the atom; everything scales up from here.
:::

## [Activation functions: a short history]{.lang-en}[活性化関数の小史]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/activations.png){fig-align="center" width="66%"}

::: {.lang-en}
- **tanh / sigmoid** (1980s): smooth, nice derivatives — good for the early learning rules.
- **ReLU** $=\max(0,x)$ (2012–): cheap, doesn't saturate — the deep-learning workhorse.
- **GELU / SiLU** (today): smooth ReLU-like; the standard in transformers.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
- **tanh / シグモイド**（1980年代）：滑らかで微分が扱いやすい — 初期の学習則に好適。
- **ReLU** $=\max(0,x)$（2012年〜）：安価で飽和しない — 深層学習の主力。
- **GELU / SiLU**（現在）：滑らかなReLU様 — トランスフォーマーの標準。
:::

::: {.notes}
Corrected from the SP25 spoken version (which dated Swish as "last 5 years"): just present GELU/SiLU as today's standard, no fragile dating. The nonlinearity is the whole reason depth buys anything — we'll prove that in the XOR block. g must be nonlinear or the network collapses (Block 4).
:::

## [Distributed representations]{.lang-en}[分散表現]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/sp25/catdog_reps.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

::: {.lang-en}
A concept isn't one node — it's a **pattern of activity across many units**. "Cat" and "dog" are nearby points in a feature space (snout size, body size → pitch, timbre).
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
概念は一つのノードではなく、**多数の要素にまたがる活動パターン**。「猫」と「犬」は特徴空間内の近い点（鼻の大きさ・体の大きさ → 音高・音色）。
:::

::: {.notes}
The deck's signature running example (SP25). A concept = a pattern, not a symbol. Two payoffs on the next slide. This is where "learned features" becomes concrete: the network discovers a space in which similar things are near each other.
:::

## [Distributed vs localist — why it matters]{.lang-en}[分散 vs 局在 — なぜ重要か]{.lang-ja}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.lang-en}
**Distributed** (a pattern over units):

- **noise tolerance for free** — flip one unit, the pattern survives
- **interpolation** — points between "cat" and "dog" are meaningful
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**分散**（要素上のパターン）：

- **ノイズ耐性が無料** — 一要素が反転してもパターンは残る
- **補間** — 「猫」と「犬」の中間点も意味を持つ
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.lang-en}
**Localist** (one node per concept):

- transparent, but **brittle**
- no natural notion of "between"

The distributed view is what makes **word embeddings** possible.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**局在**（概念ごとに一ノード）：

- 透明だが**脆い**
- 「中間」の自然な概念がない

分散的な見方こそが**単語埋め込み**を可能にする。
:::
:::
:::

[📋 Lake scorecard: distributed reps buy **similarity** and **interpolation** — but *not* **compositionality** by themselves.]{.lang-en .dim}[📋 Lake採点表：分散表現は**類似性**と**補間**をもたらすが、それ自体では**構成性**は得られない。]{.lang-ja .dim}

::: {.notes}
Two-column contrast (structural parallelism → columns per the visual-density rule). The payoff — word embeddings — is the bridge two slides ahead, via the vectors interlude, and to Mikolov 2013 (a presentation candidate this week). Lake scorecard #1: distributed reps give similarity and interpolation, but NOT compositionality on their own — mark that. Next: the zero-linear-algebra on-ramp — we've been SAYING "points in a space"; now we make it concrete.
:::

## [Data become vectors]{.lang-en}[データがベクトルになる]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/data_to_vector.png){fig-align="center" width="78%"}

::: {.lang-en}
Machines only eat numbers — so **measure**: this bento weighs 500 g, crunch 8/10. The list of measurements $[500, 8]$ is a **vector**; each measurement is a **component**; the number of components is the **dimension**. A 2-D vector *is* a point on a plane — plotting data and "representing" data are the same act.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
機械は数しか食べない — だから**測る**：この弁当は500g、サクサク度8/10。測定値のリスト $[500, 8]$ が**ベクトル**；各測定値が**成分**；成分の数が**次元**。2次元ベクトルは平面上の点*そのもの* — データを描くことと「表現する」ことは同じ行為。
:::

::: {.notes}
The zero-LA on-ramp begins (students don't have linear algebra — every concept gets a worked number and a picture; textbook prerequisite chapter: deep/vectors-and-spaces). Define vector/component/dimension on the concrete bento. Say it plainly: the cat/dog "feature space" three slides ago WAS this — we just made it honest. No Greek, no generality yet.
:::

## [Similarity is direction: the dot product]{.lang-en}[類似性は方向：内積]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/dot_product_worked.png){fig-align="center" width="74%"}

::: {.lang-en}
Multiply matching components, add them up: $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 3{\times}4 + 4{\times}3 = 24$ — the **dot product**. Divide by the arrows' lengths ($5 \times 5$, by Pythagoras) and you get $0.96$: **cosine similarity** — *pointing the same way* = similar. And look back: the neuron's $\sum_j w_{ij}a_j$ **is a dot product** — every unit scores *how similar its input is to its weights*.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
対応する成分を掛けて足す：$\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 3{\times}4 + 4{\times}3 = 24$ — **内積**。矢印の長さ（ピタゴラスで $5 \times 5$）で割ると $0.96$：**コサイン類似度** — *同じ方向を向く* = 似ている。そして振り返ると：ニューロンの $\sum_j w_{ij}a_j$ は**内積そのもの** — どの素子も*入力が自分の重みにどれだけ似ているか*を採点している。
:::

::: {.notes}
Fully worked arithmetic on the slide — no abstraction. Then the retro-link that makes the neuron slide click: the weighted sum IS a dot product, so a unit = a similarity detector for its weight pattern. This one sentence is the highest-leverage LA payoff in the deck. (Length/norm defined via Pythagoras in the figure caption band.)
:::

## [Drive it — bentos as vectors]{.lang-en}[操作してみる — ベクトルとしての弁当]{.lang-ja} {.widget-slide}

<iframe class="widget-frame" src="widgets/vector-space.html"></iframe>

::: {.notes}
Live widget (loads with tonkatsu-A/B preselected: arrows nearly parallel, cosine ≈ 0.99, worked arithmetic shown). Best contrast demo: tonkatsu-B vs salad (cosine ≈ 0.78 — dissimilar); middle case: tonkatsu-B vs hamburger-B (≈ 0.84). Toggle normalize for scale vs direction (mega-katsu vs tonkatsu-A: different lengths, same direction — same KIND). Teachable wart: all-positive features compress cosine upward — tonkatsu-A vs hamburger-A still reads 0.95; real systems center features first. This is the geometry all of today's models live in.
:::

## [Words as vectors: king − man + woman ≈ queen]{.lang-en}[単語をベクトルに：king − man + woman ≈ queen]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/embedding_arith.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

::: {.lang-en}
Learn a vector per word from co-occurrence (word2vec, Mikolov et al. 2013) and **analogies become arithmetic**. The features weren't designed — they were **learned**. This is the representational substrate every LLM is built on.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
共起から単語ごとにベクトルを学習（word2vec, Mikolov et al. 2013）すると**類推が算術になる**。特徴は設計されたのではなく**学習された**。これがすべてのLLMの表現的土台。
:::

::: {.notes}
The word2vec payoff — concrete evidence that learned features capture structure hand-design would miss. Ties to Mikolov 2013 (presentation candidate). Note honestly: analogy arithmetic is real but imperfect and dataset-dependent — don't oversell. This closes REPRESENT I; next we ask how the weights are found.
:::

# [Learn I — the perceptron]{.lang-en}[学習 I — パーセプトロン]{.lang-ja} {.section-break background-image="../../sds-reveal/sds_frame.png" background-size="cover"}

::: {.notes}
Block 3, LEARN. Point at the "how do we find it?" region of the master map. Build the simplest learner (perceptron), then the universal idea underneath it: gradient descent, which we've already met as an idea in Week 10.
:::

## [The perceptron: a linear classifier]{.lang-en}[パーセプトロン：線形分類器]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/sp25/decision_line.png){fig-align="center" width="56%"}

::: {.lang-en}
Rosenblatt (1958). Output $y = \operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x})$ — score the input's **similarity to the weight vector** (the dot product you just met), and $\operatorname{sign}$ reports which side of the **decision line** you're on. Learning = **moving the line**.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
Rosenblatt (1958)。出力 $y = \operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x})$ — 入力と**重みベクトルとの類似度**（さっき学んだ内積）を採点し、$\operatorname{sign}$ が**決定線**のどちら側かを報告する。学習とは**線を動かすこと**。
:::

::: {.notes}
Perceptron as the atom-with-a-decision — now stated in the vectors-interlude vocabulary: w·x is a similarity score, the boundary is where the score crosses zero (w is the line's normal). Define sign() at first use. The learning question: how do we move the line to reduce errors? Answer = gradient descent, next.
:::

## [Error-driven learning = gradient descent]{.lang-en}[誤差駆動学習 = 勾配降下]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/sp25/gradient_curve.png){fig-align="center" width="52%"}

::: {.lang-en}
Define an **error** $E$ (how wrong the outputs are). Walk **downhill** on $E$: nudge each weight in the direction that lowers it, stop where the slope is zero. $\eta$ = **learning rate** (step size).
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**誤差** $E$（出力がどれだけ間違っているか）を定義。$E$ の**坂を下る**：各重みを $E$ が下がる方向に少し動かし、傾きがゼロで止まる。$\eta$ = **学習率**（ステップ幅）。
:::

::: {.notes}
Gradient descent as "walk downhill on the error." Week 10 already used gradient descent as an idea (min-norm, early stopping, NTK's "trained by GD") — accurate to reference it. η is the step size. Next slide makes the callback to Q-learning's α explicit.
:::

## [You've seen this update before]{.lang-en}[この更新則は見たことがある]{.lang-ja}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.lang-en}
**Q-learning (Week 8):**
$$Q \leftarrow Q + \alpha\,\big(\underbrace{\text{target} - Q}_{\text{error}}\big)$$
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**Q学習（第8週）：**
$$Q \leftarrow Q + \alpha\,\big(\underbrace{\text{目標} - Q}_{\text{誤差}}\big)$$
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.lang-en}
**The delta rule (today):**
$$w_j \leftarrow w_j + \eta\,\underbrace{(t - y)}_{\text{error}}\,x_j$$
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**デルタ則（今日）：**
$$w_j \leftarrow w_j + \eta\,\underbrace{(t - y)}_{\text{誤差}}\,x_j$$
:::
:::
:::

[Same shape: **new = old + (step size) × (error) × (who's responsible).**]{.lang-en}[同じ形：**新 = 旧 + （ステップ幅）×（誤差）×（誰の責任か）。**]{.lang-ja}

::: {.notes}
Verified callback: Week 8 DID teach Q(s,a) ← Q + αδ with α as the learning rate (I checked the deck). Same update shape, so η ↔ α lands honestly. The delta rule for a linear output is just this. The extra x_j is "which input was responsible" — apportioning credit, the seed of backprop's blame-apportionment. This is one beat, no build-up needed.
:::

## [Anatomy of the delta rule]{.lang-en}[デルタ則の解剖]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/delta_rule_anatomy.png){fig-align="center" width="72%"}

::: {.lang-en}
For a general activation $g$, the update also carries a $g'$ term — "correct for how fast the unit is changing." That $g'$ factor is exactly what will **propagate backward** through a deep net.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
一般の活性化 $g$ では更新に $g'$ の項も入る — 「要素がどれだけ速く変化するかを補正」。この $g'$ 因子こそ深層ネットで**逆向きに伝播**するもの。$g'$ は $g$ の微分。$t$ は目標、$y$ は出力。$x_j$ は入力。
:::

::: {.notes}
The anatomy figure labels the three pieces. Introduce g' (derivative of the activation) here — it's the hook for backprop. Foreshadow: in a multilayer net, this g' term is what gets chained backward. Don't derive backprop yet — that's Block 4 after we motivate WHY we need layers.
:::

# [Learn II — depth & backpropagation]{.lang-en}[学習 II — 深さと誤差逆伝播]{.lang-ja} {.section-break background-image="../../sds-reveal/sds_frame.png" background-size="cover"}

::: {.notes}
Block 4. Motivate depth with XOR (the historical crisis), show why stacking linear layers is useless, resolve with nonlinearity, then backprop as blame-apportionment — and land the punchline that backprop IS automatic differentiation, introducing jax.grad (JAX's autodiff tool) here as new. NB: they have NOT used jax.grad before — the course used GenJAX's inference API, not raw gradients — so present it as a first introduction, not a callback.
:::

## [Quick poll — the limits of a straight line]{.lang-en}[小テスト — 直線の限界]{.lang-ja} {.poll-slide}

::: {.lang-en}
A single perceptron draws **one straight line**. It can learn AND and OR. Which can it **not** learn?
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
単一パーセプトロンは**一本の直線**を引く。ANDとORは学習できる。**学習できない**のは？
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.lang-en}
- **A.** NAND (not-and)
- **B.** XOR (exclusive-or)
- **C.** it can learn all three
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
- **A.** NAND（否定論理積）
- **B.** XOR（排他的論理和）
- **C.** 三つとも学習できる
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Commit before reveal. New poll for SP26 (the SP25 bank has no NN questions — verified). The answer is B: XOR is not linearly separable, and that single fact nearly killed neural networks for a decade (Minsky & Papert 1969). Hold the reveal.
:::

## [Reveal]{.lang-en}[答え]{.lang-ja} {.poll-reveal}

[**B — XOR.**]{.lang-en .yellow}[**B — XOR。**]{.lang-ja .yellow}

::: {.lang-en}
No straight line separates XOR's two classes. Minsky & Papert (1969) proved it — and argued important abilities (like judging whether a shape is *connected*) need exactly this. Neural-network research went quiet for over a decade.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
XORの2クラスを分ける直線は存在しない。Minsky & Papert (1969) がこれを証明し、重要な能力（図形が*連結*かの判断など）にはまさにこれが必要だと論じた。ニューラルネット研究は10年以上停滞した。
:::

::: {.notes}
Land the historical stakes. XOR is the canonical non-linearly-separable problem. The "connectedness" example is Minsky & Papert's own. This sets up the resolution: depth + nonlinearity. Show the separability panel next.
:::

## [Why XOR is hard]{.lang-en}[なぜXORは難しいか]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/sp25/xor_separability.png){fig-align="center" width="66%"}

::: {.lang-en}
AND and OR: one line separates the classes. XOR: **no line works** — the two "true" corners are diagonal from each other.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
ANDとOR：一本の線でクラスが分かれる。XOR：**どの線もダメ** — 二つの「真」の角が対角にある。
:::

::: {.notes}
The AND/OR/XOR panel (SP25, timeless). Make sure they see WHY: XOR's positive cases are opposite corners. Natural fix: add a layer. But — next three slides — depth alone isn't enough; you need the nonlinearity.
:::

## [One more tool: the matrix]{.lang-en}[もう一つの道具：行列]{.lang-ja} {.bigger}

::: {.lang-en}
Adding a **layer** means transforming *every* input vector at once. The machine that does that is a **matrix** — and multiplying by one is just **a dot product per row**:

$$\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0\\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3\\ 4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2{\times}3 + 0{\times}4\\ 0{\times}3 + 1{\times}4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}6\\ 4\end{bmatrix}$$

[The first **column** is where $[1,0]$ lands; the second is where $[0,1]$ lands — the matrix moves the whole plane.]{.dim}
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**層**を足すとは、*すべての*入力ベクトルを一度に変換すること。それをやる機械が**行列** — 掛け算は**行ごとの内積**にすぎない：

$$\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0\\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3\\ 4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2{\times}3 + 0{\times}4\\ 0{\times}3 + 1{\times}4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}6\\ 4\end{bmatrix}$$

[第1**列**は $[1,0]$ の行き先、第2列は $[0,1]$ の行き先 — 行列は平面全体を動かす。]{.dim}
:::

::: {.notes}
Zero-LA on-ramp, part 2. Define matrix-vector multiplication as "a dot product per row" — reusing the one operation they now own. Work the arithmetic aloud: the example stretches the weight axis ×2. The dim line is the deep intuition (columns = where the basis arrows land) — the widget makes it tangible next. Notation lock-in: from here, W means a matrix, Wx means "transform x."
:::

## [Drive it — a matrix moves every point]{.lang-en}[操作してみる — 行列は全ての点を動かす]{.lang-ja} {.widget-slide}

<iframe class="widget-frame" src="widgets/matrix-transform.html"></iframe>

::: {.notes}
Live widget. Drag the four sliders: the grid, the unit square, and the bento points all move — one machine, every point. Hit the presets (rotate, stretch, shear). Watch the readout: e1 lands at the first column, e2 at the second. THEN press "apply ReLU" and let them see the plane FOLD onto the positive quadrant — say "hold that fold in mind; it's about to matter." That's the whole nonlinearity story, pre-loaded.
:::

## [Does stacking layers help? (1/3)]{.lang-en}[層を重ねれば解決？（1/3）]{.lang-ja} {.bigger}

::: {.lang-en}
Try two **linear** layers, one after the other:
$$\mathbf{h} = W_1\mathbf{x}, \qquad y = W_2\mathbf{h}.$$
Surely two layers can do more than one?
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**線形**の層を2つ、続けて試す：
$$\mathbf{h} = W_1\mathbf{x}, \qquad y = W_2\mathbf{h}.$$
2層なら1層より多くを表せるはず？
:::

::: {.notes}
Build-up slide 1 of 3 (sibling slides, not fragments — this is a real derivation with three beats per the visual-density rule). Just set up the two-layer linear composition. Suspense: does depth buy anything?
:::

## [Does stacking layers help? (2/3)]{.lang-en}[層を重ねれば解決？（2/3）]{.lang-ja} {.bigger}

::: {.lang-en}
Multiply it out — two machines run in a row are **one machine** (matrix × matrix is just another matrix):
$$y = W_2(W_1\mathbf{x}) = \underbrace{(W_2 W_1)}_{\text{one matrix } W'}\,\mathbf{x} = W'\mathbf{x}.$$
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
展開すると — 続けて動かす二つの機械は**一つの機械**（行列×行列はやはり一つの行列）：
$$y = W_2(W_1\mathbf{x}) = \underbrace{(W_2 W_1)}_{\text{一つの行列 } W'}\,\mathbf{x} = W'\mathbf{x}.$$
:::

::: {.notes}
Build-up 2 of 3. The algebra: two linear layers collapse to a single linear map W' = W2 W1. Let it land visually before saying the consequence.
:::

## [Does stacking layers help? (3/3)]{.lang-en}[層を重ねれば解決？（3/3）]{.lang-ja} {.bigger}

[**Depth alone buys nothing** — it's still one straight line.]{.lang-en .yellow}[**深さだけでは何も得られない** — やはり一本の直線。]{.lang-ja .yellow}

::: {.lang-en}
The fix is the **nonlinearity**: put an activation $g$ between the layers,
$$\mathbf{h} = g(W_1\mathbf{x}),$$
and the composition can no longer collapse — **that** is why depth needs $g$.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
解決策は**非線形性**：層の間に活性化 $g$ を挟むと
$$\mathbf{h} = g(W_1\mathbf{x}),$$
合成はもう潰れない — **これ**が深さに $g$ が必要な理由。
:::

::: {.notes}
Build-up 3 of 3 — the punchline. Stacked linear layers = one linear layer, so depth is useless WITHOUT nonlinearity. This retroactively explains why the activation function mattered (Block 2). The nonlinearity between layers is the whole ballgame. Next: it actually solves XOR, and you can drive it.
:::

## [Depth + nonlinearity solves XOR]{.lang-en}[深さ+非線形性でXORが解ける]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/sp25/space_warp.png){fig-align="center" width="58%"}

::: {.lang-en}
A nonlinear hidden layer **warps the space** so the two XOR classes become linearly separable — then the output layer draws its line in the warped space.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
非線形の隠れ層が**空間を歪め**、XORの2クラスが線形分離可能になる — その後、出力層が歪んだ空間で線を引く。
:::

::: {.notes}
The space-warp intuition (SP25). Hidden units learn a new representation (learned features again!) in which the problem is easy. This is REPRESENT and LEARN meeting: the network learns features that make the function findable. Straight into the widget so they can feel it.
:::

## [Drive it — can your net learn XOR?]{.lang-en}[操作してみる — あなたのネットはXORを学べる？]{.lang-ja} {.widget-slide}

<iframe class="widget-frame" src="widgets/xor-playground.html"></iframe>

::: {.notes}
Live widget. First switch to "Linear only" and hit Train — it visibly fails (loss stalls, a point stays wrong): that's Minsky & Papert on screen. Then switch to "2 ReLU hidden units," Train, and watch the boundary bend to solve it. If time, hand-set the hidden weights with the sliders to build the solution manually. The point: the hidden layer's nonlinearity is what makes it work.
:::

## [How do we train the hidden weights? Backprop]{.lang-en}[隠れ層の重みはどう訓練する？ 誤差逆伝播]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/sp25/backprop_3layer.png){fig-align="center" width="56%"}

::: {.lang-en}
**Backpropagation** (Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, 1986): run the input forward, measure the output error, then **apportion the blame backward** — each hidden unit's share is how much it fed into the error (that $g'$ term, chained by the chain rule). In very deep stacks those $g'$ factors multiply and can shrink toward zero — the **vanishing-gradient** problem — which is why modern nets add residual connections and normalization (Block 5).
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**誤差逆伝播**（Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, 1986）：入力を順伝播し、出力誤差を測り、**責任を逆向きに配分** — 各隠れ要素の取り分は、それが誤差にどれだけ寄与したか（連鎖律で連なる $g'$ の項）。非常に深い積層ではこれらの $g'$ が掛け合わさりゼロに縮みうる — **勾配消失**問題 — だから現代のネットは残差接続と正規化を加える（ブロック5）。
:::

::: {.notes}
Define backprop at first use (no prior week taught it — verified). Intuition over derivation: it's blame-apportionment via the chain rule; the g' term from Block 3 is what propagates. Name Rumelhart/Hinton/Williams 1986. Flag vanishing gradients briefly — fixed today by residual connections + normalization (the corrected modern framing, not SP25's vague version).
:::

## [Backprop is just automatic differentiation]{.lang-en}[誤差逆伝播とは自動微分にすぎない]{.lang-ja} {.smaller}

::: {.lang-en}
You've used JAX all term. Meet its autodiff tool, `jax.grad`: hand it a function, get back the function's gradient — the chain rule, automated.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
今学期ずっとJAXを使ってきた。その自動微分ツール `jax.grad` を紹介：関数を渡すと、その関数の勾配が返る — 連鎖律の自動化。
:::

```python
import jax, jax.numpy as jnp

def loss(w, x, t):                      # a tiny network's error
    y = jnp.tanh(x @ w)                 # forward pass
    return jnp.mean((y - t) ** 2)       # squared error

grad_fn = jax.grad(loss)               # <- reverse-mode autodiff = backprop
g = grad_fn(w, x, t)                   # the gradient, one call
w = w - 0.1 * g                         # one gradient-descent step
```

::: {.lang-en}
**Reverse-mode autodiff** — what `jax.grad` computes — *is* backpropagation. Backprop is not a bespoke algorithm; it's the chain rule automated, in one call. No hand-derived update rules.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**逆モード自動微分** — `jax.grad` が計算するもの — が*まさに*誤差逆伝播。逆伝播は専用アルゴリズムではなく、連鎖律の自動化を一回の呼び出しで行うだけ。手計算の更新則は不要。
:::

::: {.notes}
FIRST real introduction of jax.grad — do NOT claim they've "run backprop all term." The course used GenJAX's inference API (.simulate / .importance), not jax.grad directly, so introduce it here as a new tool: it's JAX's autodiff, and reverse-mode autodiff IS backprop. The demystifying payoff: backprop isn't a separate, mysterious algorithm — it's the chain rule automated, one jax.grad call, and gradient-based inference/optimization everywhere rests on the same primitive. Don't run this as a validated cell in the deck — it's illustrative; the point is conceptual unification. Correct the SP25 error out loud: backprop is very much still how nets are trained.
:::

# [Represent II — architecture as prior]{.lang-en}[表現 II — 事前分布としてのアーキテクチャ]{.lang-ja} {.section-break background-image="../../sds-reveal/sds_frame.png" background-size="cover"}

::: {.notes}
Block 5. Back to the master map's "features" box, but now the point is: the ARCHITECTURE is an inductive bias — a prior over which features are easy to learn. CNN and RNN each bake in one assumption; attention relaxes them and gives the transformer. This is the run-up to the LLM block.
:::

## [Architecture is an inductive bias — a prior]{.lang-en}[アーキテクチャは帰納バイアス — 事前分布]{.lang-ja}

::: {.lang-en}
A fully-connected net treats every input the same. Real architectures **bake in an assumption** about the data — which is exactly a **prior** (the Bayesian word from Week 4 onward).

- **CNN:** nearby pixels matter together, and the same pattern can appear anywhere.
- **RNN:** the data is a **sequence**; process it one step at a time.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
全結合ネットは全入力を同等に扱う。実際のアーキテクチャはデータについての**仮定を組み込む** — それはまさに**事前分布**（第4週以降のベイズの言葉）。

- **CNN：** 近くのピクセルは一緒に効き、同じパターンはどこにでも現れうる。
- **RNN：** データは**系列**；一歩ずつ処理する。
:::

::: {.notes}
The unifying claim of this block, and a callback to the whole Bayesian spine: architecture = inductive bias = prior. CNN and RNN are two priors. Frame both as "what invariance did we bake in?" This reframes deep learning inside the course's probabilistic story rather than as a separate topic.
:::

## [CNNs: bake in translation invariance]{.lang-en}[CNN：並進不変性を組み込む]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/sp25/conv_kernel_arith.png){fig-align="center" width="58%"}

::: {.lang-en}
Slide one small **kernel** across the image and reuse its weights everywhere (**weight sharing**). A cat is a cat wherever it appears — **translation invariance**, built in rather than learned from scratch.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
小さな**カーネル**を画像上で滑らせ、その重みをどこでも再利用（**重み共有**）。猫はどこに現れても猫 — **並進不変性**を、ゼロから学ぶのではなく組み込む。
:::

::: {.notes}
CNN in one slide: convolution = sliding a shared-weight kernel; the payoff is translation invariance for free. Define kernel/weight-sharing/translation-invariance at first use. If the convolution GIF salvaged, could show it, but the kernel-arithmetic figure is enough. This is a prior: "features are local and position-independent."
:::

## [RNNs: bake in sequence — but a bottleneck]{.lang-en}[RNN：系列を組み込む — だがボトルネック]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/sp25/elman_srn.png){fig-align="center" width="52%"}

::: {.lang-en}
Feed the hidden state back in at each step (Elman, 1990) — the net carries a memory of what came before. But everything must squeeze through **one hidden state**, step by step: a famous **bottleneck**. RNNs learned *local* structure well and *global* structure poorly.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
各ステップで隠れ状態を戻す（Elman, 1990）— ネットは過去の記憶を運ぶ。だが全てが**一つの隠れ状態**を一歩ずつ通らねばならない：有名な**ボトルネック**。RNNは*局所*構造をよく学び、*大域*構造を苦手とした。
:::

::: {.notes}
RNN in one slide: recurrence = a prior that the data is sequential; the cost is the sequential bottleneck (one hidden state, processed in order — slow, and long-range dependencies fade). "Local but not global" is the SP25 Mozer-music finding, compressed to its lesson. This is the cliffhanger attention resolves. (If running long, this slide is the drop candidate per the outline.)
:::

## [Attention: a soft dictionary lookup]{.lang-en}[アテンション：ソフトな辞書引き]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/attention_lookup.png){fig-align="center" width="62%"}

::: {.lang-en}
Instead of one bottleneck, let **every token look at every other token**. Each token issues a **query**; it's matched against every token's **key** — the match score is a **dot product**, the same similarity you met this morning. The **softmax** of those scores weights a blend of the **values** — the same softmax from Week 9, sharpness $\beta$ and all.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
一つのボトルネックの代わりに、**全トークンが他の全トークンを見る**。各トークンが**クエリ**を出し、全トークンの**キー**と照合する — 一致度は**内積**、今朝学んだのと同じ類似度。そのスコアの**ソフトマックス**が**値**の混合を重み付ける — 第9週と同じソフトマックス、鋭さ $\beta$ も含めて。
:::

::: {.notes}
Attention as soft lookup. Define query/key/value at first use. THE callback that pays off Week 9: the softmax here is the same softmax/Boltzmann policy (verified — Week 9 taught softmax with rationality β). High β → hard lookup (argmax); low β → uniform blend. Every token sees every token → no sequential bottleneck. Drive the widget next.
:::

## [Drive it — attention as lookup]{.lang-en}[操作してみる — 辞書引きとしてのアテンション]{.lang-ja} {.widget-slide}

<iframe class="widget-frame" src="widgets/attention-lookup.html"></iframe>

::: {.notes}
Live widget. Click a query token, show the attention weights as bars. Then drag the sharpness β slider: at low β it's a mushy average, at high β it snaps to a single token — a hard lookup. Same knob as Week 9's rationality β. Tie back: soft, differentiable lookup is what makes attention trainable by backprop.
:::

## [The transformer: attention + MLP, stacked]{.lang-en}[トランスフォーマー：アテンション+MLP、積層]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/transformer_block.png){fig-align="center" width="42%"}

::: {.lang-en}
One block = **self-attention** (mix information across tokens) + a **per-token MLP** (transform each), wrapped in **residual connections** and **normalization** (the vanishing-gradient fixes). Stack $N$ of them. No recurrence, no bottleneck — this is the architecture behind every modern LLM.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
1ブロック = **自己アテンション**（トークン間で情報を混ぜる）+ **トークンごとのMLP**（各々を変換）を、**残差接続**と**正規化**（勾配消失の対策）で包む。$N$ 個積む。再帰なし、ボトルネックなし — すべての現代LLMの背後にあるアーキテクチャ。
:::

::: {.notes}
The transformer block, assembled from parts they now know: attention (just met) + MLP (Block 4) + residual/norm (the vanishing-gradient fixes, named in the backprop slide). Emphasize what it dropped: no recurrence. This is the architecture of every LLM. Now the last block: what happens when you make it huge.
:::

# [Understand — scale, emergence, in-context learning]{.lang-en}[理解 — スケール・創発・文脈内学習]{.lang-ja} {.section-break background-image="../../sds-reveal/sds_frame.png" background-size="cover"}

::: {.notes}
Block 6, UNDERSTAND — the whole-pipeline question of the master map, and the modernization payoff. Scaling laws → emergence (with the mirage caveat) → in-context learning taught as a LIVE Bayesian debate, not settled fact. This is the block the textbook Phase D chapter is built from.
:::

## [Scaling laws: bigger is (predictably) better]{.lang-en}[スケーリング則：大きいほど（予測通り）良い]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/scaling_laws.png){fig-align="center" width="82%"}

::: {.lang-en}
Test loss falls as a **straight line on a log-log plot** against parameters, data, and compute (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022). Performance is, to a surprising degree, **predictable from scale alone** — no new idea required.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
テスト損失は、パラメータ・データ・計算量に対して**両対数プロットで直線**として下がる（Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022）。性能は驚くほど**スケールだけから予測可能** — 新しいアイデアは不要。
:::

::: {.notes}
Scaling laws: power-law loss decrease, straight on log-log. Define log-log if needed. The striking claim: much of progress is buying scale, not new ideas — this is the compute-not-ideas point McClelland made to me in 2013, now quantified. Connects to Week 10's "scaling-laws through-line" (accurate — Week 10 mentioned it). Sets up emergence.
:::

## [Emergence — and a caveat]{.lang-en}[創発 — と注意点]{.lang-ja}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.lang-en}
Some abilities appear to switch on **suddenly** past a scale threshold — arithmetic, multi-step reasoning — abilities the smaller model seemed not to have at all ("**emergent abilities**").
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
一部の能力は、あるスケール閾値を超えると**突然**現れるように見える — 算術、多段推論 — 小さいモデルには全く無かったように見えた能力（「**創発的能力**」）。
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.lang-en}
**Caveat (Schaeffer et al. 2023):** some "emergence" is a **mirage** of the metric — switch to a smoother score and the jump becomes a gentle curve. Real or measured? Still debated.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**注意（Schaeffer et al. 2023）：** 一部の「創発」は指標の**蜃気楼** — 滑らかな尺度に変えると、急上昇は緩やかな曲線になる。本物か測定の産物か？ 議論中。
:::
:::
:::

[📋 Lake scorecard: in-context learning is real **learning-to-learn** — adapting from a few examples — one of Lake et al.'s four asks. Whether it's *compositional* is exactly the debate on the next slide.]{.lang-en .dim}[📋 Lake採点表：文脈内学習は本物の**学習の学習** — 少数の例からの適応 — でLake らの4つの要求の一つ。それが*構成的*かは、まさに次のスライドの議論。]{.lang-ja .dim}

::: {.notes}
Emergence, taught honestly with the counter-evidence in the same breath (the "teach it critically" rule). Define emergent abilities at first use. The Schaeffer et al. mirage result is essential — do not present emergence as settled. This models the epistemic stance for the next slides on ICL. (Skippable live if short; stays for the recording.)
:::

## [In-context learning: learning without weight updates]{.lang-en}[文脈内学習：重み更新なしの学習]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/icl_setup.png){fig-align="center" width="66%"}

::: {.lang-en}
Give a **frozen** model a few examples in its prompt — *plip→blue, plap→red, plip→?* — and it continues the pattern. Nothing was retrained; the "learning" happened entirely **in the context window**.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**凍結**したモデルにプロンプト内でいくつか例を与える — *plip→青, plap→赤, plip→?* — とパターンを続ける。再訓練は一切なし；「学習」はすべて**文脈窓の中**で起きた。
:::

::: {.notes}
Define in-context learning at first use: the model adapts from prompt examples with NO weight update. This is genuinely strange — it looks like learning but the parameters are frozen. Poll next asks them to locate where the learning "lives," then the Bayesian lens (and its critics).
:::

## [Quick poll — where did the learning go?]{.lang-en}[小テスト — 学習はどこへ？]{.lang-ja} {.poll-slide}

::: {.lang-en}
A frozen LLM picks up a made-up rule from 3 prompt examples. Where does what-it-just-learned **live**?
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
凍結したLLMが3つのプロンプト例から作り話のルールを覚える。今学んだことは**どこにある**？
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.lang-en}
- **A.** in updated weights
- **B.** in the context window — weights unchanged
- **C.** in a retrieval database
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
- **A.** 更新された重みの中
- **B.** 文脈窓の中 — 重みは不変
- **C.** 検索データベースの中
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Commit before reveal. New SP26 poll. Answer B — the weights never change; the adaptation is entirely in the activations conditioned on the prompt. That's what makes the Bayesian reading tempting: conditioning on examples, not updating parameters, looks exactly like inference. Reveal, then the debate.
:::

## [Reveal]{.lang-en}[答え]{.lang-ja} {.poll-reveal}

[**B — in the context window; the weights never change.**]{.lang-en .yellow}[**B — 文脈窓の中；重みは変わらない。**]{.lang-ja .yellow}

::: {.lang-en}
Conditioning on examples without updating parameters looks a lot like **inference**, not training. That resemblance is the basis of a striking — and **contested** — claim.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
パラメータを更新せず例で条件付けることは、訓練というより**推論**によく似ている。この類似が、印象的で — かつ**議論のある** — 主張の根拠。
:::

::: {.notes}
Land the framing: ICL = conditioning, not gradient learning. That's the hook for the Bayesian interpretation. Next slide states the claim; the slide after gives the counter-evidence. Both on screen — this is a debate we're teaching, not a result we're endorsing.
:::

## [The Bayesian lens — and its critics]{.lang-en}[ベイズの視点 — とその批判者]{.lang-ja}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.note-card .ink}
::: {.lang-en}
**The claim — ICL $\approx$ implicit Bayes.** Pretraining fits a **prior** over latent patterns; the prompt's examples are **observations**; the continuation is the **posterior predictive**. Pretraining is *empirical Bayes* — estimating the prior itself from data. [(Xie et al. 2022; Ye et al. 2024)]{.dim}
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**主張 — 文脈内学習 $\approx$ 暗黙のベイズ。** 事前学習は潜在パターン上の**事前分布**を当てはめ；プロンプトの例は**観測**；継続は**事後予測**。事前学習は*経験ベイズ* — 事前分布そのものをデータから推定。[(Xie et al. 2022; Ye et al. 2024)]{.dim}
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.note-card .ink .warn}
::: {.lang-en}
**The pushback — the math doesn't check out.** If prompt examples are exchangeable (order shouldn't matter), the running prediction must be a **martingale**: no systematic drift as examples arrive. Real LLM predictions **violate** that. [(Falck et al. 2024)]{.dim}
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
**反論 — 数学が合わない。** 例が交換可能（順序は無関係）なら、逐次予測は**マルチンゲール**でなければならない：例が増えても系統的に漂動しない。実際のLLMの予測はそれを**破る**。[(Falck et al. 2024)]{.dim}
:::
:::
:::
::::

[The lens is *suggestive*, not settled — and it's the payoff of everything from **Week 4's hierarchical Bayes** onward.]{.lang-en .yellow}[この視点は*示唆的*であり確定ではない — そして**第4週の階層ベイズ**以降すべての成果でもある。]{.lang-ja .yellow}

::: {.notes}
THE modernization slide and the seed of textbook Phase D. Teach it as a live debate — Xie/Ye's ICL-as-Bayes formalization (pretraining ≈ empirical Bayes: optimizing marginal likelihood of sequences) AND Falck et al.'s martingale counter-evidence, both on screen. This is the honest epistemic status: a workshop-level formalization with active refutation, not a textbook fact. The callback to Week 4 hierarchical Bayes is the reason this course earns this slide — the reader has the prior/posterior-predictive machinery already. Do NOT overclaim.
:::

A pretrained model predicts text; making it **helpful and safe** is a second step — **RLHF** (Week 9): fit a reward model to human preferences (Bradley–Terry), then RL the policy. Same inverse-RL machinery, now aimed at values.

- **Next week (Week 12):** ethics, fairness, adversarial examples, alignment.

事前学習モデルはテキストを予測する；それを**有用で安全**にするのは第2段階 — **RLHF**（第9週）：人間の選好に報酬モデルを当てはめ（Bradley–Terry）、方策をRLで最適化。同じ逆強化学習の仕組みを、今度は価値に向ける。

- **来週（第12週）：** 倫理・公平性・敵対的事例・アラインメント。

Bridge to Week 12 via a verified Week 9 callback (Week 9 DID teach RLHF/DPO with Bradley-Terry — checked). Pretraining gives capability; alignment (RLHF) shapes behavior; next week is the ethics/safety of that. Keeps the whole-course arc intact: IRL → RLHF → alignment.

## [One question, four answers]{.lang-en}[一つの問い、四つの答え]{.lang-ja} {.big-figure}

![](images/four_answers_close.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}

::: {.lang-en}
"Where does the hypothesis space come from?" — penalize complexity (**ridge**), grow with data (**BNP**), a prior over functions (**GP**), or **learn the features** (neural nets). The first three fix the kernel; the fourth learns it — and at infinite width, it circles back to a **GP** (Week 10).
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
「仮説空間はどこから来るのか？」 — 複雑さを罰する（**リッジ**）、データとともに増やす（**BNP**）、関数上の事前分布（**GP**）、または**特徴を学習する**（ニューラルネット）。最初の三つはカーネルを固定；四つ目はそれを学習 — そして無限幅では**GP**に戻る（第10週）。
:::

::: {.notes}
The closing picture — the same master map, all four answers annotated. The satisfying loop: the neural-net answer, taken to its infinite-width limit, becomes the GP answer from last week (NNGP/NTK). One coherent story across two weeks, not two separate topics. This is establish-then-reference paying off.
:::

## [Lake's scorecard, settled]{.lang-en}[Lakeの採点表、締め]{.lang-ja}

::: {.lang-en}
Back to the reading — now with 2025 evidence. Deep nets deliver **learned representations**, **similarity**, and **scale** — genuinely. What Lake et al. (2017) say is still missing: **compositional generalization** and **causal, model-based** understanding. Even meta-learned nets reach human-like systematicity only with effort (Lake & Baroni, 2023), and a 2025 re-test of **multimodal** LLMs on Lake's own domains — intuitive physics, causality, intuitive psychology — still finds them short of people (Schulze Buschoff et al., 2025).

**The honest verdict:** the 1988 → 2017 → 2025 critique still bites *and* learned features are powerful. Both are true.
:::
::: {.lang-ja}
課題論文に戻る — 2025年の証拠とともに。深層ネットは**学習された表現**・**類似性**・**スケール**を確かに提供する。Lake et al. (2017) がなお欠けていると言うもの：**構成的汎化**と**因果的・モデルベース**の理解。メタ学習ネットでさえ人間並みの体系性には努力を要し（Lake & Baroni, 2023）、2025年の**マルチモーダル**LLMの再検証 — Lake自身の領域（直観物理・因果・直観心理）で — も、なお人間に及ばないと示す（Schulze Buschoff et al., 2025）。

**正直な評価：** 1988 → 2017 → 2025 と続く批判はなお有効で*あり*、学習された特徴も強力。両方とも真。
:::

::: {.notes}
Settle the scorecard honestly — the "fact-check attributions" rule. Lake & Baroni 2023 is the right nuance (meta-learning CAN reach compositional generalization, but it's not free). The 2025 update is Schulze Buschoff et al., *Visual cognition in multimodal large language models* (Nature Machine Intelligence, Jan 2025): they tested vision-based LLMs on Lake's exact core domains — intuitive physics, causal reasoning, intuitive psychology — and found they "still fall short of human capabilities," explicitly framed as a follow-up to Lake's proposed domains. This is also this week's presentation-candidate paper, so a student may be presenting it. Don't declare a winner. The course's stance: hold both the power and the critique, now across a 1988 (Fodor & Pylyshyn) → 2017 (Lake et al.) → 2025 (Schulze Buschoff et al.) arc. This is the intellectual honesty that distinguishes this lecture from a hype reel.
:::
